utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For a change, I will open the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Seric:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Aguirre, you said you studied law in San Sebastian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You graduated in 1993. That's what you stated, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you start your postgraduate studies immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started my studies in Notre Dame in the States in '94, in August '94, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please speak up for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your postgraduate studies have a specialisation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My studies, a Master's degree that I got in Notre Dame, was a Master's in peace studies, the matter of which was primarily international relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were -- you had been to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was that during your studies, during some break in your studies? That's what I didn't understand quite.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been there on different occasions, so the first visits were before I was graduated, as you can see. And then I continued and I went there on different occasions after I graduated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that you went to the territory of the former Yugoslavia as a student? Were those tourist trips, or could they be characterised in a different way?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but not only as a student.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of your visits to the countries of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already mentioned in my first intervention on Wednesday, the main purpose of my visits, or the most relevant one here, was for humanitarian matters. I was working for a humanitarian organisation, organising activities such as convoys, delivery of basic supplies in refugee camps in the war areas. And the visit, as I say, was to assist the humanitarian situation and to try to organise some of the projects of this nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which refugee camps did you visit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many, a number of them, some of them located in Croatia, and others located in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So among them were, for example, the refugee camp of Gasinci, which was, at the time, one of the biggest refugee camps in Croatia. A number of camps in the area in Dalmacija, in the area around Split and other places of Dalmacija. Then I certainly visited refugee centres in the city of Mostar, for example among them, the students -- a students' djacki dom, a students' house, residence, in Mostar, and other centres in the municipality of Capljina, others in other cities of Central Bosnia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was accommodated in refugee camps in Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the refugee camps were under the authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, by any chance, what population was placed there, to what ethnic group they belonged?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of the population in those camps were Bosnian Muslims, Muslims coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when this indictment was brought against Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Object to beyond the scope of direct examination and relevance, Your Honour. This witness testified simply to the foundation of certain documents tendered by the Prosecution, and that is the only subject that he testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric, I would like to remind you that this witness is not a fact witness but a document-foundation witness. I hope you could draw our attention to certain documents presented through this witness. Yes, Mr. Seric [sic]? I'm surprised that you're standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have to respond to this objection. If we have no knowledge of facts, we -- one cannot recognise documents and documents cannot be tendered to this Trial Chamber. So we do have to verify the facts and the knowledge, the scope of knowledge, of this witness to establish whether he has knowledge about the documents which may be tendered because the documents cover the period from 1992 to 1994. This gentleman told us how long he was in Bosnia and what he was doing there. I think that in our cross-examination, the Defence has the right to verify his knowledge about the facts from the documents he is speaking to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also object procedurally. I don't know why Mr. Krsnik is on his feet during the cross-examination by Mr. Seric. And we continue our opposition. It's irrelevant and beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric; do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Thank you, Mr. President, for allowing me to finally get the floor after the objection of my colleague, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm trying to establish a background for further questions, considering that this witness participated in the gathering of evidence against my client, Mr. Vinko Martinovic. So his work and his procedure is not [as interpreted] relevant because he is a member of the team of one of the parties to these proceedings. Therefore, his knowledge about the indictment and his method of work, as I am trying to establish, were within the framework of the same indictment. If we can stipulate this, I can simply skip over my next 10 or 15 questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, you have to understand that we have got a lot of documents through this witness. I think the main purpose of this cross-examination is to try to ask some questions to this witness about the authenticity of these documents. I hope you could concentrate on your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all right. I will abide by your decision, but the fact is that this witness was expressing his opinion on the consistency with international law and international humanitarian law and the international laws of war, and it is my duty to establish or to refute the consistency of his statements. But if the witness said that he knows the features and characteristics of international war legislation, and that he's able to recognise something as being or not being an international conflict, then it is my duty to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the best of my recollection -- and if it's necessary to go through the transcript, we can do this. To the best of my recollection, this witness testified to nothing about the consistency of international law or international humanitarian law. I don't remember any such testimony. He testified about the documents, the nature of the documents, whether the documents were consistent with similar documents that he'd seen, that one HVO report looked like similar HVO reports, the format was similar. And I must object again. And as I forecast last week, Your Honour Mr. President, in fairness -- as I forecast last week when this issue came up, I would be on my feet a lot. And I will tell the Chamber now I will be on my feet a lot this morning if the cross-examination goes beyond the scope of direct. And the only reason this witness was tendered was as a procedural witness on the foundation of documents. And I will continue to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Scott. Mr. Seric, opinion of this witness on certain issues is not so important to us. We just want to know your questions concerning with those documents. You may proceed along this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aguirre, you stated that the events from 1993 were consistent with the book of Mr. Tudjman called, "Nationalism in Modern Europe," published in 1981. How did you arrive at that conclusion? Did you read this book in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with due respect, that's not what I stated. What I said, that there was a coincidence in between the places, the geographical locations, mentioned in the exhibit, in the document 1 of this collection, and the places, the locations, mentioned in other documents. The conclusion can be drawn just by reading the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read other books by Mr. -- Dr. Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you chosen this book yourself as one of the pieces of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. evidence presented by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not selected this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you, in your work as an investigator, worked consistently with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, just for the sake of accuracy, my work is the work of an analyst, and the answer is yes, I have worked for the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just said that your work is that of an analyst. Who gathered the documents?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents contained in this collection were gathered by different members of the Office of the Prosecutor. In some occasions, attorneys were involved. In other occasions, investigators or also analysts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you then testify to the authenticity of these documents if you don't know how they reached you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with your respect, I do know how they reached us. I can explain you how I know that. This is part of my regular work in the Office of the Prosecutor. The main source to ascertain the origin of the documents is simply our databases. We can check this against the databases and then find out who gave the document to us, when, and who received it from our side. That's how we can find out that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this work, in the gathering of this documentation, has really all the documentation referring to the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina been gathered?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, sir, all the documentation will never be gathered by anybody. This is not a realistic expectation, I would say, with due respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- let me start this way: In your work on this documentation, did you work after November 1998? Did you continue working on it after November 1998?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, in terms of percentages, what share of documentation was covered by you after this date in relation to the overall quantity; 50 percent, more, less?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For what concerns the recollection, gathering the documents, I believe that they haven't been involved in the gathering of any of these documents. This can be checked. We can ascertain and determine who received each of them. It happens -- it is actually a coincidence. It could have happened that I gathered them. But this particular collection was gathered by other members of the Office of the Prosecutor, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This gathering of documents, was it done mostly after November 1998?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, I believe on the contrary. Those were gathered mainly before. I would need to check in detail the databases to give you the most precise answer, but we have to see that the main source, the majority of the documents originate from UN - United Nations - sources. And those were mainly -- those included in this collection were gathered at an earlier stage. A number of them were gathered in '96, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I need some time since I skipped over a number of questions in view of your decision. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Kresimir Krsnik, Defence counsel for the accused Naletilic. I will be dealing mainly with documents which I hope I have studied in detail, and I hope you will be able to follow my questions. Similarly, I will try to make my questions as concise as possible, and I expect the same of your answers. Let us start with a few general questions. My colleague has already touched upon certain matters. I would like to ask you specifically what criteria were used and who selected the documents with which you, as member of the Prosecution team, you prove this international conflict? So what criteria were used and who made the selection?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I will do my best to assist you. The selection was made mainly by members of the Prosecutor's office. Only to discuss by sections, as I explained, the collection comes from different origins. So when we received documents by governments, by the state authorities, either, for example, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the authorities of Croatia, it is the submitter, the provider who is making their own selection. That happens. Anyway, such documents are a minority -- or a minor component of this collection. In other instances, when we have access to the collections ourselves, we make the selection ourselves, the officer who is in charge for such an action. That is particularly the case when we work in the state archive of Croatia. We can select ourselves. There is also the case when we have access to a number of collections of the United Nations, collections of the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia in Geneva, or collections of the headquarters of UNPROFOR in Zagreb. We are given access -- we can enter and select the documents. That is also the case for documents coming from the Spanish army, from the headquarters of the Spanish army. By the way, I wonder if this is something that can be stated in open session, but -- well, that is the case in such selection of documents. As for the criteria, well, there are several issues. One important issue is the presence of units of the army of Croatia in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We know -- we have information available, originally from open source, from different sources, that identifies a number of units. So if you see in a document, for example, that is mentioned the HV Brigade Number 116, just as an example, you would certainly make the judgment that this is a relevant document and you would select it. Another criteria is the presence of commanders, commanding officers of the army of Croatia that were acting -- they had a commanding -- a position of command in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have the names of those. We have the names of certain people that we believe that it is the case that they were commanders of the army of Croatia. If we see that name mentioned, we will select it, and so on and so forth. I think I have given you a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely what I think we should discuss, because all my further questions follow from that. As regards archives and the United Nations, we will talk about that later and elaborate this topic. I'm interested now in the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You said that they, among others, selected some documents. Before that, I think I should ask another question. Who was it who decided, and who decides, which out of the host of documents should be presented here as evidence? And by what criteria? Are there, by the same token, other documents which you also got from the same source and which tell a different sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour the Prosecution team selects those documents, primarily the lawyers, and I would object to go beyond that under Rule 70. This goes into the internal work product of the Office of the Prosecutor. And it is the lawyers who make the ultimate selections for trial and mark the exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, this question should be answered by the witness himself. It seems that you give the answer by yourself. That's not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness's other microphone please be turned on? The booths have trouble hearing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We too also have some problems with the earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For this particular case, for each case, the selection is made by the trial team, and particularly by the attorneys. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of the question was: Have we received all the documents that you got and that are related to this subject, or are there other documents as well? Are there some who tell a different story as compared to those that you have given to us?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are more documents, certainly. There are actually many more documents. I believe that -- well, it is the normal procedure, it's the obligation of the Prosecutor, to deliver documents that could have an impact on the Prosecutor's case, I mean potential exculpatory documents. So your question, I understand, refers to such a duty, and I believe that that duty has been, well, duly complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, of course, it was no accident that I'm putting this question. Although our time was short, we studied these documents that we got in depth. However, there is a question that arises: Why have some documents not been signed, why have some been submitted only in part? Why have some been translated only in part? So what happened with the other parts? So why were only parts of documents given rather than entire documents? If one studies the entirety of these documents, one comes to a different conclusion. Even if these documents -- on the basis of these documents that you did give us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think counsel -- if that's the allegation, counsel should take the witness to a particular exhibit. I think it's unfair to ask him about 97 exhibits all at one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite agree with you. Mr. Krsnik, you have to lead this witness to a particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, let me bring the witness to this. We have worked on this three days and three nights. I have got all of this on paper, and now I am just trying to broach the matter in principle, from a general point of view, and I would kindly ask my learned friend to be a bit more patient. It's not only one document. There are several of them. Of course, I'm going to go into all of that. I want to deal with some questions in general. My question is whether the gentleman, the witness, knows about this, and I'm asking him for an explanation. Why have some documents been submitted in part and why have some been translated in part? I think it is such a simple question. If the witness knows the answer, well and fine. If he doesn't, again, well and fine; then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber also shares the concern of yours. We also found that certain documents have some problems. I hope you could lead to particular documents, to ask this witness to make some clarification on those documents, rather than asking such general questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall abide by your guidelines. I shall not be long in this introduction but I think it is necessary for you, Your Honours, to broach the subject matter appropriately. All right. We are going to skip this particular question altogether now, until we get to more specific matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, tell me, which are these authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially those that gave you documents, which are these authorities? Who are you referring to? Oh, yes, I beg your pardon, and also, which year or years are you actually referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. The authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina delivered 21 documents of this collection of a total of 97. There are different authorities; some are judicial authorities, there is the police, and there is also the agency for international communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps my English is not very good, but it says "Bosnian government" everywhere. Doesn't that mean Bosnian government, government in the sense of cabinet, administration?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it says where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your list of documents. That's why I put this question to you. "Bosnian government." Which Bosnian government and which years are we talking about? 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these documents are usually provided by the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what the reference means. The originator, say, one step behind the submission, can be then different agencies within the authorities, within the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date it goes from -- 1996 would be, I believe, the earliest submissions, including this collection, up to 1998, and maybe beyond as well. Certainly I believe that most of them came from the period in between 1996, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what the setup in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in '92, and '93, and then at the time of Dayton and after Dayton and nowadays? Speaking of nowadays, do you know if a state of Bosnia-Herzegovina exists nowadays?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it exist in '93, 4, 5, the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need -- to answer your question, I will need to deal with some issues that go beyond the submission of documents and information contained in the binders. But the short answer is yes, it did exist but in a different form. Before the Dayton agreements, it was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after, it was simply the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the short answer in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who represented the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Witness, in 1993, 4, and 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to the question, Your Honour. Again, it is beyond the scope. The witness has already testified that the earliest of these documents came in 1996. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this does not go beyond the scope, because if the origin of these documents is the Bosnian government, we have to ascertain which Bosnian government and who stands behind these documents. This is a crucial issue. Of course, I don't want to put questions and answer them because we have not revealed before this Trial Chamber what the political situation in '93, 4, and 5 in Bosnia-Herzegovina actually was. I would like the witness to say that. We are going to deal with it when the time comes for our case, but I think it is also right for the witness to say that in connection with these documents because if he is speaking about the Agency for Documentation, this is the famous AID, it is a secret police, a secret police that we have to know more about, and it is important for the Trial Chamber to understand this fully. So my question is, who represented Bosnia-Herzegovina in '93, 4, and 5? Let us not deal in delusions or deceptions here. Who represented? Then we're going to realise it was only the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I continue to object to the relevance, Your Honour. Counsel can put their case. They can put their Defence case on when it comes to their case. With the Chamber's permission, they can call as many political witnesses as they think they want to, subject to your approval. That is not the purpose of this witness. He did not talk about the politics in Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1993, 1994, 1995. It is far beyond the scope of this witness's purpose for being here. And again, we are getting far afield. This is not the Defence case. They can put this case on if they wish, with the Chamber's permission. That is not this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I think your question is too broad. It's very difficult to answer, even if the witness knows the answer, because it's a very long period from '93 to '95, who represents the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a very complicated question. We understand that that government have underwent a lot of changes. You may ask a particular moment, a particular time frame concerning with a particular document. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Of course, I don't want to take up my time, but when we studied the documents and we looked at the submitters, we saw "Bosnian government." So my question was only who was the Bosnian government in '93, 4, and 5? Nothing else. Who is this Bosnian government? Is it the result of elections; is it a legitimate government? These are the questions. I think that everybody has understood what I'm asking. It is not as if somebody were a self-styled government proclaiming himself to be a government, saying, "I am the government." It is a very simple question, and that is what the witness put here under "Submitter," "Bosnian government." Well, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please, you closely collaborated with the Agency for Information and Documentation. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, among others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Honourable Trial Chamber which organisation is this? What kind of an organisation is this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, as far as I could see, this is the agency in charge of the investigation of war crimes by the Bosnian side, the Bosnian authorities. So for what concerns our work, they are the people who were gathering evidence relevant for war crimes. Not the only ones, but they have this -- I would say they have this specialised orders certainly among their duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your activities, you did not come to realise that this was an intelligence, counterintelligence organisation, secret police, that deals in the kind of matters that such services deal with, instigation of unrest and various other activities that such organisations involve themselves in, frame-ups, et cetera? Didn't you come to realise that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the characterisation. Assumes facts not in evidence. There is not evidence that supports the questions put by counsel. He is injecting completely political issues into the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This question is allowed, but you should not put an answer in your question, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise if that was your understanding. I just asked, since the gentleman closely cooperated with them, and he said that he did -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let us hear what is the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sir, first of all, I would like to clarify that the input of such agency for this collection is a minor one. It's a very minor part of the whole collection. As I said, 21 documents come -- were delivered, were provided by the Bosnian authorities, meaning actually the Bosnian Embassy Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in The Hague. And I believe that only part of those 21 could have been originally formed or delivered by such agency. Now, I am happy to give you my opinion, my assessment, on the Agency for Information and Documentation. Our experience with them for what concerns our work has been positive. Our experience with them for what concerns documents has been also positive in the sense that I have never found a document provided by such source that could have been -- that appeared to be either manipulated, changed, or in any way suspicious. That is the truth of my experience with such agency. About other duties that are apparently assigned to such agency, I cannot comment. I have not worked in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how many documents did you receive from the AID for this case? Of course, if you know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to answer. I really can't say that off the top of my mind. A number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these documents were taken from, where they were kept, under which conditions they were submitted, who needed them in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Where were they taken from? That was my first question. How did the AID come across documents that absolutely have to deal with the Croat side? Did they steal them? Do you know how they obtained them? Do you know what their origin is, what their authenticity is? It is my understanding that you get these documents here in The Hague from the embassy. Is that the only thing you know, or do you know who wrote them, what their source was, where they were kept, where they were taken from?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, is this question related to these particular documents or in general to any documents submitted by them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon. It's my fault. I didn't spell the question out concretely enough. You are the witness for these documents, but you said that you were an analyst otherwise as well. So may I ask you about other documents, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to that. Beyond the scope, completely beyond the scope and also guarded by Rule 70. I direct the Chamber to Rule 70(A).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, you may ask any questions concerning these documents, but it seems that you are beyond the scope to ask about other documents. By the way, your question is quite complicated. It's a compound question. Would you please ask those questions one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these documents were created, the documents that you got through the AID? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what concerns this collection, I know that they were submitted by the Bosnian authorities. I cannot give you exactly -- I cannot tell you exactly which one was delivered by the AID or by a judicial body or by the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I know that they were submitted by the Bosnian government, meaning the Bosnian embassy in The Hague. I know that, in general, their sources are such, but I cannot give you the answer for each particular document in this collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. We may therefore infer that you know nothing about the source of documents.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can infer that, but I think it's not a reasonable inference. I will explain you why. I will need to explain a bit of my work. In short, we basically have -- deal with three areas when we deal with the documents: The authenticity of the document, the reliability of the source, and the credibility of the information contained in the document. We need to consider the three elements together. It may be the case that you have doubts on one of the areas, but if, for example, you have a doubt on the credibility of the source but nevertheless the document appears to be authentic and the information appears to be credible, you may consider that it is worth to submit the document, that the document is still acceptable and relevant. So that can be the case. I think the Chamber will be best assisted if we discuss the documents on which you are concerned one by one. So the Bosnian authorities submitted documents. As I said, I believe this makes a total of 21 documents. Seven documents within these 21 came from the Travnik police department. And these are -- these refer to applications for citizenship of Croatia in 1992. One document, it's an open document, is a letter from Izetbegovic to Tudjman. Other documents are HVO documents. I believe that 12 HVO documents were submitted by the Bosnian authorities. So even if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, may I interject, dear colleague? I do have questions along those lines, along what you have just mentioned, so we will deal with it one by one. I just wanted to discuss sources in principle - I mean where the document was created - because you get these documents here in The Hague and then, of course, you assess the documents, and then you see whether you believe they are authentic, et cetera. We have had witnesses who have assessed the authenticity of documents, experts in the field, but this is what I wanted to clarify here. You get these documents here in The Hague but do you know specifically what goes on in the ground? So perhaps we did not understand each other properly. When I said "source," I mean the actual source of the document. Perhaps you misunderstood what I was asking. Now, why am I asking you this? You assert that the commanders of the HV - I'm not talking about the HVO, I'm talking about the HV - that they were commanders in the HVO. So I'm going to ask you the following: How do you know this? On what is this assertion of yours based?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question can be answered partly by reference to the documents contained in the collection. The documents refer to such persons in particular, they are named there, and it is reported that they are commanders within the HVO. Then, in addition to this, we will need to refer to other sources that are not included in the collection, but those are known to me through my work, those are based in evidence available to the Office of the Prosecutor. I would like to direct your attention particularly to the documents that are -- that originate from the book by General Bobetko. This is a clear source of evidence that is showing commanders of the army of Croatia asserting command over the HVO. You can see this in the documents and you can see that General Bobetko himself is issuing orders to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dear sir, 1992 and the possible activity of the Croatian army was based on an intergovernmental agreement signed between the B and H and the Republic of Croatia at that time. And do you know that this agreement was signed and also carried through? Are you aware of this document? Because I did not find it among the documents that were submitted to us.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware. I mean, in my view, your comment is relevant about -- is relevant for the legitimacy but that's not questioning the international character of the matter. That comment could assist to judge the legitimacy of such intervention or not, but that's not questioning the fact that the intervention did happen as such. That's my assessment of this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the basis of the agreement reached between the two governments, and on the basis of the request for assistance that was put forth by the BH in 1992, a military agreement was signed. It's the military agreement I was referring to. Are you aware of this document? Have you seen this document? If so, why did you not put it in here? Because it explains all of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, objection, Your Honour. We are again way off the nature of the documents. In the last answer, for instance, there were questions about the legitimacy of the Croatians' presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina during 1992. That is far afield from the authenticity of this particular document. We are again getting into wholly different matters. This witness cannot express a view on the legitimacy at any particular moment of Croatia's presence in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, let's hear first why that agreement was not included. Witness, you may answer this question, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. As I said before, I did not make the selection of the documents. This -- I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our distinguished colleague certainly knows this better than I do, but as for 1992, we have almost 20 documents from 1992 that primarily deal with the book of Janko Bobetko. 24 - my colleague has just corrected me - 24 documents. I think that it is indeed relevant because, otherwise, why are they in this collection of documents? And also, Your Honours, there was a certain consistency that was referred to in respect of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm going to put the following question to you, dear colleague: Do you know, for example, what citizenship Josip Praljak has? Whose citizen is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, can counsel take me to a particular document where Josip Praljak is mentioned? Out of the 97 documents, can he please take me to that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. It's Slobodan Praljak, actually. It was my mistake. We have both in this case. This one is Slobodan Praljak. Mr. President, one of them, you know, was referred to in connection with the camps, and Mr. Slobodan Praljak is a general also mentioned in these documents. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is: Do you know which citizenship he has?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean the document number 59?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And document 60, Your Honours; 59 and 60.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer? First, we will need to qualify the question; at which point of time? Because I believe this change or this may have changed throughout time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the time since there have been citizenships. You know when states were created in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and you know which state he belongs to. Once acquired, citizenship is citizenship. Let us not go into legal issues in this regard.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. Is there some way that the citizenship of Mr. Praljak is related to Exhibit 59 or Exhibit 60?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you may explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, and with pleasure, Your Honours. One of the proofs of international conflict, according to the Prosecution, is that Croatian officers took part in the HVO, were present in the HVO, and that's the reason for my question. That's why I'm asking about the citizenship of Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I truly am sorry. I know probably I'm trying the Court's patience. Again, I forecast this last week. Counsel, they can put in their defence case. They can call all the witnesses they want. They can call Slobodan Praljak if they want to. That is beyond the scope of this witness. This witness came and testified about 97 documents. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you have to understand that this is the first time for us to touch upon a specific document, and that's what the Trial Chamber want to hear. No matter this witness knows or not, we would like to hear the answer. You may answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that it is the case that Slobodan Praljak enjoyed both citizenships of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. He was a native from Capljina. He was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina of Bosnian-Croat origin, and I believe that later he acquired the citizenship of Croatia. This was the case with many Bosnian Croats, as you can see in the documents. The documents that I mentioned before of the Travnik police show how hundreds of applications were forwarded for this matter, for citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Bosnian-Croat origin in order to gain the citizenship of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. I'm trying to make it clear to the Trial Chamber what was going on and to establish the truth, and I'm asking for your assistance in this effort. Do you know -- when Yugoslavia existed as Yugoslavia, until certain states were recognised as independent, do you know how many Bosnian Croats were involved in the Croatian army when the Yugoslav army attacked Croatia? How many of them came to defend Croatia within Yugoslavia? Do you have any knowledge about that? I'm trying to make this short and to make us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. Now we're talking about fighting in a whole different country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree with Mr. Scott. Mr. Krsnik, it's out of the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, we cannot conduct an examination in this way because I am doing this for your sake because you need to understand in all objectivity all the events that took place in that territory. We have to understand these issues. It is not an accident that Praljak was involved in the HVO. It didn't happen out of the blue. It has its own history, a background that we have to understand. One shouldn't be allowed to claim in this courtroom that Croatia carried out aggression, and I want to make it clear through this witness to you, because there is a logical, historical truth in this respect. If the witness is not aware of it, then let it be. We'll move on. My second question was, how many -- excuse me, Mr. Scott. How many Croats who had the citizenship of Croatia but whose motherland is Bosnia, how many of them came back to Bosnia to defend the country? They number in the thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the problem with this is, again, fundamentally -- we have said this many times now since last Wednesday. And counsel -- the problem is they can, again, put this evidence on in their own case if they wish. That is beyond the scope of this witness. The problem with this cross-examination is not because I'm on my feet; it's because counsel insist on cross-examining beyond the scope of both the direct examination and the particular role for which this witness was tendered. They may want to, in their case, call all sorts of soldiers who fought the Serbs in Eastern Croatia. If the Court wants to hear about that, it can, but that is beyond the scope of this witness, Your Honour. And that's the fundamental problem here, and counsel persist in asking questions that are beyond the scope of direct examination and this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honours, I have the record of the examination-in-chief right here. Mr. Witness answered, The consistency of documents with the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was also confirmed by the fact that Mr. Praljak was assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. And we got this answer in the examination-in-chief. Is that right? I'm just testing his knowledge about Mr. Praljak and the documents which confirmed this consistency because I am challenging this consistency. It doesn't exist, and I'm trying to make it clear before the Trial Chamber. I cannot do that unless we go back a little. I'm not jumping suddenly to 1991 for no reason at all. Who are those officers from the Croatian army involved in the HVO? And the witness did speak about that in the examination-in-chief. My question was very simple; does he know how many citizens, citizens of the Republic of Croatia who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina came to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina against the Serbian aggression? It's a very simple question; does he know, doesn't he know? If he does know, let him share it with us. That's how we will arrive at an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we believe that you have full right to defend your client in your direct examination at a later stage. And this witness is available in the OTP in The Hague, and you can call this witness as your witness in your direct examination, if you want to make sure what happened in certain period of time. But the purpose of this cross-examination should be strictly within the scope of the direct examination. I hope you could skip this question and continue your cross-examination. What we are interested is the particular documents in those two binders. As I mentioned earlier, we also have some doubts concerning certain documents in those two binders. We want to seek an explanation from this witness so as to dispel our doubts on those documents. This is the main purpose of this cross-examination, and it's the purpose for this witness to be with us today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're moving on right now, Mr. President. With the assistance of Madam Registrar and the usher, I would like to show this witness the first binder containing documents from number 1 to number 60.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you kindly take document number 53. Could you please turn to page 3 of this document, item (e). My first question: You did not have this document in the Croatian language available to you. Does the Croatian version exist in your Office of the Prosecutor? Because this is a Croatian document, if you look at it. I think it was signed by the president, Mr. Franjo Tudjman. The original is in Croatian, that's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a procedural matter. I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Because we haven't received it, and that's a little strange. But never mind. Item (e). As you can see, it says that there is [In English] Agreement between Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republic of Croatia, signed 21 July, 1992. [Interpretation] Did you find that document dated the 21st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could assist me on this one, what does it --

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find this document, I didn't check it, because it's not a fact in contest. This is clear and there is no -- it's not a controversial fact, such an agreement. The agreement in itself, I don't find it a controversial fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Can we move to item 3 of this same document, closer to the bottom, after item (e)? It's followed by item (f), then point 3, and the last paragraph. Which number of refugees Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is mentioned here? Is that consistent with what you know? The number is 650.000 refugees of Muslim - that is Bosniak - ethnic group, and the providing of security for these people. Is that consistent with what you know?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is consistent, what is agreeable, is that a large number of Bosnian refugees and Bosnian Muslim refugees were received in Croatia. That is consistent. The particular number, exact number, was an issue. It was a controversial issue. There were different estimates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it consistent that the Croatian army should be deploying -- was deploying its troops along the border in a state of alert, in a state of war? Is it consistent that they should be deploying their troops along the borders of other states?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Consistent with what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you should be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my question that I always asked: Consistent with what? What I mean here is consistent with the facts that this witness is aware of, because that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I will refer to my criteria for consistency or for evaluating the documents. The first point we need to take into account for this particular exhibit is the originator. I would not consider the president of the Republic of Croatia a credible source for this particular matter. The duty and the -- well, yes, the duty of the president of the republic is to defend the interests of the republic, rather than to report objectively on the situation. The president of the republic had an interest on this particular matter. So I think that the credibility of this source is arguable, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this letter, I think, was addressed to the Security Council of the United Nations. Do you mean to say that the president was informing the United Nations in a less-than-objective way, that he was disinforming them, or what? Because this letter is addressed to the Security Council. What worries me, though, is why is there no signature on such an important letter written by a statesman. So there are two questions. The first, if I understood you correctly: Would the president of a state, even if it were a banana republic, allow himself to behave in that way towards the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Object to speculation, Your Honour. The reason this document was submitted, Your Honour, again it's the Security Council record. It is not, and it does not purport to be, the original, the original letter, in the Croatian version. If counsel has that, I invite him to put it into the record. I won't object if he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we have to know some working procedures in the United Nations. There are six languages in the United Nations, as official languages. If a country does not use those -- one of those six languages, they have to submit their documents into one of the six languages. That's why, at letterhead of this document, it says, "Original English version." This is the first thing. Another thing is that we believe that this document has been distributed among all the members, at least, of the Security Council. There must be a signature in this document in its original form. When the United Nations distributed those -- these letters, it cannot have that signature on it. But there is no doubt that it should be regarded as an official document from the United Nations, because it's a -- it bears a serial number on there. Everybody will have access to these documents in the archive of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Thank you very much for your assistance and understanding. I wanted to go through this with the witness, especially because it's very difficult for me, when I'm talking to my client, to interpret for him each of these documents during our consultations, because my concern about this document is how we should understand this, because we cannot take out of context one letter addressed to the Security Council. And that's why I asked Question No. 2 to this witness: Does he know where the attack on Croatia came from in 1992? Who attacked it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to understand that this witness is a documentary foundation witness, not a fact witness. You could not ask the question concerning with facts to this witness. It's not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With due respect, Your Honours, please bear with me for a little. We cannot take one single document out of a pile and present it to the witness as evidence, because we will create complete confusion - that's what I'm most afraid of - because if one document is saying that, for instance, Dubrovnik was attacked from Trebinje and was bombed for a long time, then all the experts are wondering does Croatia have the right - and it does - to go 100 kilometres deep into another state to return fire? That's what I'm asking this witness. Because Croatia was attacked from Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a historical fact. It was bombed, shelled, the army came, the tanks, missiles. It all came from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it lasted until the end of 1992, until the attack, the Serbian aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina started. Zagreb was under rocket attack from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if he's speaking about these documents, he must have knowledge about that, including knowledge about General Praljak. He must have knowledge about the documents and the consistency, and he has already said that General Praljak was Assistant Minister of Defence. And we will probably bring him here. I want to make it all clear to you. It's not for my own sake, and not even for the sake of the record. That is my main intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked the Chamber to cast its eyes down this lengthy question that has gone on now for some lines in the transcript. This once and for all makes the point that the Prosecution has been trying to make; that this is beyond the scope of direct examination and beyond the purposes for which this witness was tendered. Now we are talking about the shelling of Dubrovnik. We are talking about all sorts of things. Counsel again misunderstands. If he wants to bring this evidence before the Chamber, and if the Chamber wants to hear it, he can do that. But that's not this witness. For some reason, we can't seem to get that point established. The witness did not come here to talk about any of these things, either substantive, historical, political information that this witness was not tendered for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We agree with what Mr. Scott said on this particular issue. We believe that the incidents in '91 has nothing to do with this witness in this present case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the constant discussion by my learned friend makes me want to respond, but I don't want to take up any more time because this is a legal issue. It's already 11.00, but I hope we will have time on another occasion to respond to these objections. I see that my colleague, too, doesn't understand because we come from different legal systems. These are witnesses and issues from our legal system. I think this is not understood enough. If my colleague asks a question, gets a response in the form of a statement, it's my right to react to that statement. And that's why I'm asking the question about Mr. Praljak. Otherwise, we won't be able to clarify and get to the truth. In any case, it's 11.00. I think it's time to break, if you agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you could ask this witness any questions concerning these documents, but this Trial Chamber has made a ruling that we believe the incidents in '91 has nothing to do with this witness and with the present case. You have to abide by the rulings of this Trial Chamber. You may resume your cross-examination at 11.30. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before moving on to the next document, dear colleague, I wanted to ask you as soon as we heard an interesting thought of yours concerning the document that we just looked at -- Do you hear English? No. The document was signed by Mr. Tudjman; you said that it is not of major credibility. My question is, do you think along the same lines when documents come from the Bosnian government and when they were signed by Alija Izetbegovic and others, especially with regard to such an important institution such as this Tribunal is, or rather, the Office of the Prosecutor that you work in?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, I would say yes, meaning that, in general terms, a representative of a state, if such state has an interest in the conflict, that needs to be taken into account to assess the credibility and that may affect the credibility. That is right. In this context, if I may comment, the issue had been reported before by the United Nations, which can be seen in the collection. The Secretary-General had already reported in negative terms, in critical Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. terms, against the Republic of Croatia. So there was the possibility or the possible threat, I would say, of getting some sanctions because of this matter. So it wasn't dangerous to the Republic of Croatia to either conceal or underreport the issue or present it in a way that would prevent the United Nations taking such action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have certainly understood that, but my question was something else. My question was: Did the Bosnian government behave in the same way in its own interest? Because this is a UN Tribunal and it had a significant interest in acting that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the witness already answered the question yes, Your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We also believe that this witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at document 27, please. Can you tell me what the point is of this document? Why would it be a negative thing if the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were signing a document that is supposed to lead to peace? This is a document that was supposed to bring peace to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I do not see the point of this document.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the matter for discussion is not the goodwill of the parties or the peace negotiations. The matter, I understand, is the international armed conflict. And for that matter, it does contain relevant information. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if the whole document is read, then your answer and this document are not mutually related. If you read the document in its entirety. Of course, I'm not going to read the entire document because it's self-explanatory. I have, of course, marked the most interesting details in this entire document. It absolutely speaks of peace, not international conflict. It talks about bringing peace to Bosnia-Herzegovina, dividing it into provinces, et cetera. In addition to that, the Croats actually signed it, or rather, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Very well, let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, that was a speech without a question. If there was a question there, let the witness answer. If he can give an answer as to why the document is relevant, let him. But we had about a ten-line speech and no question. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You have to put your question in the form of a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, I do apologise. I thought that I had put a question. I said: How is this document that speaks of the peace agreement, and that is supposed to bring peace, what does that have to do with the nature of the international conflict? Because the entire document has to be read, Your Honour. Of course, I don't want to read the whole thing because we are all aware of how much time would be needed for that. That is the question I put to the witness, quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the relationship between this document and a document that has to do with the international conflict?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are several points. To begin with, in this document, and other United Nations documents included in the collection, you will see that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be recognised, will be mentioned, referred to, as an internationally-recognised state, which is relevant to begin with. And the representatives will be addressed as representatives of a state member of the United Nations. This can be seen in several documents of this collection. In some documents, when they refer to the withdrawal, actually they request the withdrawal of troops of Croatia, they refer to that fact, that -- the reason is actually, the origin of this request is that Bosnia is an international-recognised state. This can be seen in this and other documents of the United Nations. More in detail, if you want, you can see point 21 in page 6 of this document, in which you can see that President Franjo Tudjman of Croatia is taking part in these negotiations. This may be relevant. As for what concerns the conflict in general, a fact is that such negotiations in January, 1993, were followed by an increase, a hardening, a worsening of the conflict. There was, well, significant increase of the conflict, of the war, in between the forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat forces. That can be also relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are not discussing the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina is an independent, internationally-recognised state. We are -- it was only a state de jure. However, its form of setup was related to these agreements because the three peoples had to agree on what the future political setup of this state would be. That is why we are asking what this has to do with the international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Next is number 28. If this document is read in its entirety, how can one conclude that It is related to an international armed conflict, especially Item 2, where reference is made to the civil war and Bozo Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need a few seconds to go through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means. I hope I'm not interrupting you, Witness. Item 1, perhaps I can lead you through the document because, indeed, I think I know it by heart. Item 1 says unequivocally that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is exclusively Muslim forces. You do see what item 1 says, don't you, and especially the last point where it says -- where reference is made to the Geneva plans and Alija Izetbegovic. Of course, if you want to read through it again, please go ahead. But my question was, how does this all relate to international conflict?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I am reading it now, I can't see direct evidence of international conflict. I think the document may be relevant in the broader context or in connection to the previous or other documents and so on. But in itself, I cannot see that it contains direct evidence to this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now go back to document number 1, please. My first question, distinguished colleague, have you personally read this book, all of it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. I have read the section included in this exhibit, exhibit includes the index, and I believe that this is the relevant section for this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this book was published and for which audience?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That you can see in the document itself. It says, it says in the first page, 1991, Columbia University Press, New York.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for what kind of readership, for what kind of audience?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe for anyone that could enter a bookstore and buy the book. I don't think it was directed against any -- it was targeting any particular audience, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this document was never printed or published in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, not until the present day, except for one single copy at the university library? And I have it right here. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does this question go to the authenticity of this document? Is Mr. Krsnik saying that this book wasn't published by Columbia University Press? What does the fact whether it was published in Bosnia have to do with the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we believe that this question is relevant, and we want to know some related matters concerning with this book. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know that there is one single copy in the English language at the university library, and nowhere else in all of Croatia -- or rather, in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia? And that is why I asked you for which audience this was and what was the subject matter involved.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the book was distributed in the former Yugoslavia, and I don't know the number of copies available in the territory of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the basic profession of Dr. Franjo Tudjman was? Do you know what his doctorate was about or in which field?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the late President Tudjman had different professions, different jobs throughout his life. Now, the interest of the point, I believe, is about history. If that's a point, yes, he did some historical research, which can be seen in the document itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an historian, did he have the right to write books and present his ideas and give comments about history? This book deals with a time period spanning from the Turkish times until the socialist Yugoslavia, socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is exactly the question, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, do you allow an historian to write books and give comments about things that happened in history in the past? He is explaining historical events. Had you read the entire book, then perhaps we could discuss it, and then we will go to these three pages that were taken out of context. But do you allow an historian to write books and to deal with a subject matter belonging to his profession? Isn't that the fundamental right of any historian?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the issue is not if he is allowed or not. The issue is what he is saying. Many things can be said about history, and some of them are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. related to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is your thinking. The thinking of Dr. Franjo Tudjman in this book coincides with your thinking, does it, on the basis of three pages from the book that were read?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you be please more precise on the question? Thinking on what exactly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that 12 years before the conflict took place, the tragic conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, are you trying to say, on the basis of three pages from a book that you read, on the basis of three pages that were taken out, you are proving the aggression of Croatia against Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is a mischaracterisation, Your Honour. Again, I thought the question was going to be a proper question until we got to the end. Then it gets all over the place again. I object to the question. Now we are trying to prove: Is it your position, Mr. Witness, that this proves the aggression of Croatia against Bosnia-Herzegovina? Mr. President, that's awfully broad, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we agree with the Prosecutor, with his objections, Mr. Krsnik. Can you skip this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can skip everything. I can finish my cross-examination as such. This book was discussed extensively during the examination-in-chief. You know that I also had some objections when this book was discussed, because it proves international conflict. So I'm asking the witness, very nicely, in his opinion, since he submitted these three pages into the file of documents that are supposed to prove an international armed conflict, does he still claim that these three pages from this book that was written for students in America - I have the entire book here, I don't want to go into all of that - that is supposed to explain how the republics and autonomous provinces in Yugoslavia came into being? Does he still think that this has to do with an international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I could phrase the question that way.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, I believe it is a relevant piece of evidence, because the author became president of the Republic of Croatia, and I will mention a point that I already mentioned on Wednesday. There is a remarkable coincidence, the geographical areas mentioned in this book and the areas mentioned in the rest of the documents, particularly the areas mentioned in the UN report where they identified units of the army of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally - you personally - know about this - and that is what you spoke of during your direct examination - that the Croat army was in that area, in those areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, it's a mischaracterisation of the evidence. There were documents tendered. If you look at the documents, they will show that various reports were made about the presence of Croatian army units in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Mostar. It wasn't this witness's opinion. It was what the documents that he testified about the foundation of said. That's beyond the scope -- expressing a further opinion is beyond the scope of direct and this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. We are not very much concerned about the opinion of this witness. We are very much concerned about the documents this witness presented to us, namely, the authenticity of the documents, the reliability of the sources, and the credibility of the information contained in those documents. This is what we are caring about. Everybody has his own opinions concerning certain incidents, but we believe that this witness's opinion is irrelevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have got this document, Your Honour. I'm not going to read from it now. The document is self-explanatory. But later we are going to tender the entire book and then the Trial Chamber will be in a position to come to its own conclusions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, if that's the case, then there is no question about its authenticity, and we just spent some minutes now talking about a document to which there is no challenge to its foundation. If counsel is going to put the same book, the entire book into evidence, I stipulate. I admit it. It can be admitted right now. There is no dispute about authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's not the time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the point is we are here to talk about whether the documents are reliable and authentic. And now counsel, he is -- the only place he can challenge this evidence, I respectfully submit, is that the document is somehow inauthentic or should not be accepted by this Chamber. That's the only purpose of which this witness testified. As you said just now, Mr. President, it is not about this witness's opinion.
