If counsel says he is going to put the entire book into evidence, then, Your Honour, respectfully, I submit then that it's obvious the case that there's no dispute about its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Krsnik, would you please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Final question with regard to this book: On the basis of three pages of a book, can you speak about the consistency of this book with documents that were created 10 or 15 years later?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can speak about the consistency of these pages with the rest of the collection. That is what I am speaking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please move on to document number 3 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I guess, then, from the last answer, that counsel doesn't want the answer to the question. He asked him if he could answer the question; the witness says he can answer, and the witness was not given any opportunity to say what it is. I leave it in the Chamber's hands, but the witness was not given an opportunity to give the answer other than to say yes, I could explain if given the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we are quite satisfied with the answer of this witness. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got document number 3? I will kindly ask you, do you see the copy in Croatian, in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had major problems in understanding it because it's highly illegible. Tell me, from which file did it come and get into this file?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was submitted by the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't this document already used in another case before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, this signature at the bottom, can you confirm its authenticity and the source of the document? We're dealing, again, with the year 1992 and the war with the Serbs when the Croats and Muslims were together. And my question is, what does this have to do with international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, point by point: About the signature, no, I cannot confirm the authenticity of the signature. About the origin of the document, as I've mentioned before, our experience is that a document submitted by the Bosnian authorities - so far I haven't come across any case of forging, manipulation or anything - our experience is that documents submitted by these sources are normally, usually authentic. That's our experience. Now, about the matter, let me take a look. This is a document addressed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. I think that this is a relevant point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a letter addressed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, that is what matches, in your opinion. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed by a military commander from a different country in the context of an armed conflict, yes, I believe it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't the Vitezit factory the point here? Was the subject of this the factory called Vitezit, in the town of Vitez, producing explosives?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, and I don't think that the document mentioned anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document and the people mentioned here, were they related to the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. I believe so. I believe this refers to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question is: What is the relationship between Central Bosnia and the indictment? And my second question, but you already confirmed this, it is just an indication as to who the letter was addressed to. And in connection with that answer of yours, my second question would be: Don't states cooperate in terms of logistics, supply of arms, et cetera? My first question, therefore, is: What is the -- how is Central Bosnia related? And my second question is: Isn't it normal for states to cooperate in purchases of arms, logistics, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Central Bosnia is related to this case, I believe, in different ways. First of all, the area of the indictment and Central Bosnia are both part of the same state, internationally-recognised state. So the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information related to Central Bosnia may be related to the matter of international armed conflict, being also part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For criminal matters, this is a different issue. I don't think -- eventually, we don't need to go into this now. For purposes of organisation, we can certainly say that Central Bosnia was an operational zone of the HVO, and as such, Central Bosnia and southern Herzegovina, Mostar, were part where we think the same structure of the HVO for matters of organisation. What was the -- oh, yes, cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik and Mr. Aguirre, can I interject? We are spending an awful lot of time on these last two documents, and having read both of them, it seems to me that all the Prosecution is attempting to show with these documents at the moment is their relationship, the relationship of the second document with the treatise, to use a neutral word, which was published by Mr. Tudjman. Surely all that this document in order is showing consistency, which has been, I think, expressed on a number of occasions by this witness, of the ideals and aspirations expressed by Mr. Tudjman in his book, and nothing more than that. It is just following this. Because Mr. Mate Boban appears to reiterate the ideals and aspirations which were mentioned in those excerpts from Mr. Tudjman's treatise. So really we are not getting anywhere if we parse the contents of this document, because you already are going to proffer the entire treatise as published by Mr. Tudjman on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Above all, the witness specified that this document cannot really attest to the international nature of the conflict, as he added it to the other documents. So these documents should be viewed together with other documents. If you want to prove this on the basis of just one document, I'm afraid we wouldn't be advancing very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we do not get translation. Sorry. Yes. You may try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your suggestions and insight, which I accept in full. Every document is different, and I want to reach some answers, such as what does this document have to do with the international armed conflict? The very fact that they contacted the Croatian Ministry of Defence seems to suffice for it to be relevant. Another matter that I wanted to resolve is we simply didn't manage to understand this document because -- to decipher it, because it's almost illegible. On the other hand, there is a translation -- or, rather, there isn't a translation. The document that we have here, we didn't succeed in establishing whether there is a translation because the English version does not coincide with what we have here. At least, we didn't manage to decipher it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, two things, Mr. President. There is a translation -- it's obvious the documents speak for themselves. This is originally a B/C/S document, which is the third page of the exhibit. There is then a French translation before it and an English translation in front of it. Now, most of it, it is the -- the third page is not certainly ideal. I think most of it - not to me, but to a B/C/S speaker and reader - can be legible, can be read, most of it. If the original -- if a further copy needs to be obtained from the purposes of the evidence vault, to see if a better copy can be provided, I'm happy to pursue that. But again, how is that a question for this witness? Now he's asking this witness about the status of translation. Again, this is simply not this witness's purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's very clear, and I'll respond to this immediately. The witness said he had analysed the documents and he had worked on them, and I will give you a specific example. This gentleman, who is signed here, we tried to establish whether the man exists, and we got the answer that there is no one by the name of Basko Ljubicic, and I want to hear this witness's answer to this. And we always used to say it's very difficult to deal with names originating from the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you have a particular question in your mind, just put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So specifically, who is Basko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not totally certain about this, but I believe the answer to this is there is some misspelling or a mistake in the transcription. Since the original document, it's true, the quality is not very good, apparently in the translation, they put a "B" where most likely there should have been a "P." Most likely the first name of this person is Pasko, with a "P."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, if you please, distinguished colleague, please look at this name in the Croatian version. Do you see it? Is it a "P" or a "B"? We don't need any translation or interpretation of this. Did you conclude on the basis of this signature that it's Pasko or Basko, either way?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, the quality of the document is not very good, so you cannot be certain about this. I infer that probably it's "P" because that is a common Croat name, and I'm familiar with such a first name, Pasko, with a "P."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can you shed some lights on those names?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you allow me - and I'll only answer if the Chamber invites me to because I don't want to be accused of testifying - but I think I can assist the Chamber by saying that the original document indeed says Pasko Ljubicic. I asked -- I'm pursuing this moment a better version of this document be brought to the courtroom. I've seen the original document myself. Because Mr. Krsnik is indeed right, it was used in another case and admitted in another case, the Kordic case, the name is Pasko Ljubicic, and a different version will be brought to the Chamber as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can now move on to Exhibit Number 5. My first question, what is that 4/4th Brigade of the ZNG and who does it consist of?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can say from the document is that it was a unit of the army of Croatia under the command of the Split operational zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reference is made here to ZNG. What is that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it is translated here, National Guards Corps. It is an early delineation for the units of the army of Croatia. It was an initial delineation in the first period of the formation of the army of Croatia, which is -- we're talking about 1991 initially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that ZNG soldiers were exclusively volunteers, and that's the reason why they were called the National Guard Corps? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the soldiers were volunteers or were not volunteers. But the issues mentioned in the document itself in point 6, the last paragraph, you can see it yourself. It says, "All HV insignia are to be removed from the fighters and present yourselves as volunteer defenders of your homeland." So what the document shows is that the regular commander is instructing his troops to present themselves as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is how you read the document. Can it be read in a different way? Can it be read as meaning that they were volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, now we're going to argue with the witness about what the document means? Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, we are not going to argue with this witness about this document. We believe that document speaks for itself. If you have any questions, you are free to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they volunteers? Because the witness is saying, on the basis of these documents, they were the Croatian army. And I'm claiming the opposite, and I'm claiming that this document is saying this clearly enough. These were people who went to Bosnia and Herzegovina as volunteers. And I hope that other witnesses will tell us more about that in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And between who and who was the war conducted, then, in the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that you would know the answer to this question. But in the year '92, the conflict took place primarily in between Serb forces and then Croat and Bosnian Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who then formed a joint army. And what is the relevance of this to the international armed conflict? That's my final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a legal issue. That is a legal issue. I'll be happy to argue it, but I assume you don't want to hear from me at this moment any more than you already have. That is a legal issue. And we will indeed -- it will have to be briefed. I assume there will be extensive submissions to the Chamber on this point. But it won't be coming from the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We agree with the Prosecutor on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it may be that Mr. Scott is right. Maybe I really don't understand the meaning of cross-examination. Because I fail to understand absolutely, after having read the transcript of examination-in-chief, where every other sentence mentioned the word "consistent" and "consistency," I thought in my cross-examination I had to challenge this claim because I believe that these documents are consistent with nothing, because this witness made a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of statements regarding consistency. And I apologise in advance to this Trial Chamber if I don't know how to properly conduct a cross-examination. I had been observing Mr. Scott and trying to learn from him. And I believe I have learned enough. But if I'm failing, please instruct me. I've spent three days and three nights over this. And I thought I was doing fairly good job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, as I said not long ago, that everybody will have his opinion on certain issues on a certain document. This witness is just to tell us the authenticity of the document as well as the reliability of the sources. He may, himself, have an opinion towards certain matters. There's no need for you to agree with this witness at all. You have the full opportunity to present your witness to challenge whatever there was in the documents and whatever is said by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understand you correctly, then there is no purpose to my further cross-examining this witness. Then I'll simply object to the tendering of these documents and we'll end it at that. I was just saying that this document is self-explanatory, and I was asking this witness why he chose it in the first place as a document confirming international armed conflict. And I wanted to clarify it in front of you. Alternatively, I can write a 24-page motion explaining why I believe it shouldn't be admitted as evidence confirming international armed conflict, and I believe that further cross-examination makes no sense. We have got to the fifth or the sixth of these documents, and there are a hundred of them. And I prepared to cross-examine him on each one of them to prove inconsistency, that is, precisely the opposite of what the witness had claimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we believe that you have reached your goal of the cross-examination. You cast serious doubts concerning those documents which has been correctly recorded in the transcript. When we are going to evaluate those documents, we'll take into consideration of your objections during your cross-examination. That's the very purpose of the cross-examination. But it is not necessary to ask this witness to entirely agree with you on certain opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate your advice. Thank you very much for sharing your insight with me, and you have assisted me a lot. I believe that after this clarification, I will, indeed -- rather, write all the rest of my arguments in a written objection, and I think we'll take at least a month doing that because we need to further study these documents in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, since we have the witness here, you may ask any questions concerning other documents, so that let us know initially which document are you objecting? This is what we want to know. And that will be correctly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to all the documents except the original documents of the United Nations, that is, resolutions, et cetera. I object to each one of them, and I challenge all of them. And that is the point of my objection -- that is the point of my cross-examination, and that's what I prepared for. I apologise, but what is the purpose of this witness in that case? These claims could have been introduced by anyone. These documents speak for themselves. For instance, I came to the book by Janko Bobetko. It's a very long book. We could discuss it for two days. Do you allow that we in Croatia know why Janko Bobetko wrote this book? It refers to year 1992. Now, I don't know what to do. I can really stop my cross-examination at this point, but it's your opinion that matters the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, it is my view that the Prosecution, through this witness, is saying that this collection of documents taken chronologically show that an international armed conflict occurred because of the presence of Croatian troops from Croatia. So it's irrelevant if they're Croatian troops, people from Herceg-Bosna of Croatian. We have been, as I understand the evidence, to be invited to draw an inference from reading these documents chronologically that this conflict was an international armed conflict because of the presence of Croatian troops on more than a few occasions, and that it was coupled with policy of the government of Croatia. And he attempts to show this by orders from Croatia generals. Now, we are very interested to know what the Defence view of this collection of documents is. It isn't necessary for you to debate with this particular witness what his interpretation of the politics behind each document is, but we take it that your view is that this Court shouldn't draw the inference we've been invited to draw from reading those documents, and hopefully, through this witness, you will be able to present in some clear way to us what the Defence case is in relation to this collection of documents. Now, are we taking you short when asking you to address it in this way? Because, obviously, it's an important aspect of your case, as you said earlier, last week. But really, that's what you ought to do, is to show through cross-examining this witness, that your view is that we should not draw the inference because of X, Y, Z, but so far, we know the position you're taking, but you haven't led us to any particular documents which you say will help to prove this thesis. I'm sorry for taking so long, but it is a very important aspect of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed, Judge Clark. I didn't even have the time - you see how time flies - but that's precisely the aspect I wanted to cover through this witness and the documents. There are two logical periods in the history of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina: That is 1993 and 1992. We have a logical approach, or rather, an invitation for Croatia to come in and help in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then we come to 1993, when that army is no longer there. And that is the subject matter I wanted to come to. These facts are common knowledge. What was their army? Who were its commanders? This was a matter of discussion earlier. Of course, the Defence will bring witnesses to prove that, because we cannot leave this issue hanging in the air, as it is now. And as for documents where we are contesting authenticity, it's a different matter. We have two or three questions about that. But how did the ZNG come into being? This witness should know that, if he has dealt with this matter. How it became about, who were members, those are things -- I mean the ZNG, the National Guard Corps. This document speaks for itself, but only if we know what ZNG means. We have to make it clear for your sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think that he told us what he understood by it, but he's not a military tactician or an analyst. He's an analyst of documents. He doesn't have to go behind the meaning of each of the documents. Now I understand you to say that there is no dispute, from your point of view, that the Croatian army from Croatia was present in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period of 1992 when the common enemy was the Serb -- were the Serbs. And so therefore you have no dispute about the documents which indicate this in 1992. If I understand you correctly, then, you should go on to cross-examine this witness on documents which you dispute in this collection and which will, I take it, from your point of view, show that there were no Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just respond? Excuse me, Mr. Scott, the question was put to me. Could you please be so kind as to let me respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy to, Mr. President, if I can then respond further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for 1992, there are documents that I first asked whether this witness knew about them, that justify my particular stand, because these were specific actions and also off-setting the fire that came from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is one aspect. Another aspect is the request put forth by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina for assistance. And that is why my question in relation to each and every one of these documents is: What does this have to do with the international conflict? And we haven't got this basic fundamental document that would explain all of this. And that is why I've been referring to 1992. And then we are going to move on to 1993, which is a different situation altogether. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I simply wanted to follow up on the response elicited by Judge Clark's questions, just to make sure, just to be clear. Do I understand, then, there is an admission that it can be taken as established for all purposes of this case, so that the Prosecution does not have to offer any additional evidence on this point, that the Croatian army was present in an armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the year 1992? Now, if that's not disputed, then -- and that's admitted, then I'll be happy to accept that admission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik? Is there a dispute concerning with this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am in a dispute with the way the Prosecution has been presenting this, and I thought that through these explanations of these documents, we are precisely going to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. get to my point: When and in which particular case? However, the way the Prosecution is presenting this is something that I am in a dispute in, yes, indeed. You see, now, this is a subject matter that I wished to broach with this witness, and that also has to do with what the indictment says, and, yes, indeed, I am challenging that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I know it's not my turn, Mr. President, however, my colleague Mr. Scott said something about the Defence, and I believe that this pertains to the Defence of Vinko Martinovic. 1992 -- and what I tried to do this morning, and I gave up after having heard what you had to tell me, if we are going to proceed from a theory, or rather, theory and practice, in terms of everything that took place in warfare, and if we take into account what Michael Akehurst said about civil wars, then it is certain that not a single civil war remained beyond international activities. So there are activities that are going -- that are taking place outside the territory where the actual war is being waged. And, of course, this has nothing to do with what the Prosecution is putting forth, and I strongly oppose this. I believe that this is something that is aimed at making us accept something that is totally unacceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add that I did not see 1992 mentioned anywhere in the indictment? It is not within the scope of the indictment at all, 1992. 1992 is only used in order to give the Trial Chamber a truthful portrayal of historical and other events. And that was my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we have already spent a lot of time on those procedural matters. We regard it as procedural rather than substantial. Do you have any questions with this witness? If you have, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to ask you if you would take into account this Defence proposal: Could we take a break now rather than at 1.00, so that I could narrow this area down with my team, and if I could see what are the questions that still remain, and in that way, I would shorten my cross-examination in keeping with your instructions, because I have a lot of questions here, about 100 questions, and if I am not mistaken, we have only reached document 6. This way, I think that we are going to gain in time because then I'm going to summarise the whole thing and shorten it as well. I think it's only 20 minutes more -- or, rather, we can start 20 minutes earlier, if it's all right with you, so I really am in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there is no objections from the Prosecutor's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is no objection to that. I would like to clarify one matter, but if my friend will give me an opportunity, I'm not going to interrupt counsel now. I have no objection to this change in schedule. I would like to address one procedural matter before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You may address that procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted the record to be clear, and we will tender to the Chamber -- I will tender to the Court staff this morning -- actually, I guess it's this afternoon now -- last week, when this witness was first called and the issues about these documents were first raised, and again throughout the course of the morning, there have been many references to the volume of these documents, the late disclosure of the documents. We just looked at these documents. Simply want to make it -- and in fact, Mr. Krsnik last week was very emphatic in saying that my representation that these documents had been turned over almost a year ago was not correct. And I will provide for the Court staff a copy of our letter, tendering the -- about 90 per cent of these documents to both counsel, dated the 8th of December, 2000, followed with a list of these documents attached. I will also then, with a follow-up letter dated the 20th of March, 2001, again asking the Defence counsel for their response to these documents, and in fact saying, We are still asking your position about these documents on the existence of international armed conflict. We understand--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. That's all, Your Honour. I simply want to -- I think it's very important, especially in the light of what's been said -- I'll slow down, Your Honour. In light of the things that have been said, Mr. President, about this collection of documents and the issues that have been raised, and I am concerned that there may be an attempt to characterise the record that these accused have not had sufficient opportunity to address the documents based on things that I am hearing. I want the record in that regard to be perfectly clear, and I am tendering these documents to the Chamber, that the vast majority of these documents were tendered to the Defence almost a year ago, on the 8th of December, 2000. I have that document here. They were then further discussed in correspondence with counsel dated the 20th of March, 2001 in which -- I signed that letter -- in which I specifically asked counsel to state their position on the international armed conflict documents. And I won't belabour it further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's another matter I would like to mention at this moment, that this Trial Chamber made a ruling concerning the translations of those documents. And we realise that today is the 12th of November; that is the deadline involved in the decision. We may give some leeway for the tendering of those documents so long as this witness was here last Wednesday. So if we cannot finish this witness and all these documents tendered through this witness, it should be regarded as was tendered last Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, to be very precise, I did tender them. And in fact, to be transparent, I was very careful that I did tender them all last Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll adjourn until 2.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have conducted additional consultations, so we will only refer to some of the documents, if this witness can clarify them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my first question, after the break - I hope you managed to get a bit of a break yourself, a bit of rest - document number 11, please. Could you please tell me the following: This document that we see here, is that also from another case before this Tribunal? And through which witness was it introduced? Who is that particular witness, and in which case, of course?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't know if this has been used before in another case. That I don't know. I know the name of the witness. Now, I would like to clarify if I am allowed to disclose this name, because it may be the case that it's a protected witness. That I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, let's move into private session, please, only for that brief answer, because I'm really interested in hearing whether this document was actually tendered in that other case and whether the origin was proven in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is the following: The use of Croat dinars in Kiseljak and throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask whether this decision pertains to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina or only the municipality of Kiseljak. There is a document and that's the way it was in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, too. That year, on the 15th of June, 1992, there was total war.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these two documents refer to the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, what was the legal tender in June 1992? What did people do in Central Bosnia? What was the currency that was being used?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that several different currencies were used at that area and time. Main ones would be the Bosnian official currency. Then we have the Croat dinar, as we can see, and then people will also use actually German marks or other currencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how is this, then, related to international armed conflict, this particular document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, in my assessment, what is relevant here is that this is not a matter of social or common use. This is an order for mandatory use. This is imposing an obligation to use such a currency. This is what is relevant. Here we see that it is an imposition of the Croat dinar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to document number 13, please. Brief question: If I have understood this correctly, this is an order, and it also says, Attention, Mr. Andabah, with an H, and also Mr. Jaganjac?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your research of these documents, was there a consistency involved in terms of was there a Mr. Andabah, say, on the 18th of June, 1992? Because in the Croatian original, it says Andabah. These are two completely different last names. Or have you included this document, thinking it is Mr. Andabak, and there is nothing to support that? In the second page of the Croatian version, again it is Mr. Andabah.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand your concern. First of all, this document comes from the book of Mr. Bobetko. The original, as you can see, is issued by General Bobetko. And then the translation, I believe, for this matter is correct. In the original, it says Andabah, and so it says in the English and the French translations. In my assessment, in my view, this is most likely a mistake, a misspelling or a typo. I have not seen an officer with this family name. I have in this context -- in a context very close to this document, I have seen an officer with the name Andabak, last letter being a K, Andabak. Most likely these documents refer to an officer with the name Zdravko Andabak who was an officer of the army of Croatia who intervened -- actually, it was a commander, not commanding officer, of the army of Croatia acting in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Zdravko Andabak?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You meant him then, did you, Zdravko Andabak?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I say, yeah, Zdravko Andabak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, this was a book that was published. It appeared in public, and nobody reacted and corrected his last name. Maybe there was a mistake in the document, but now we have this very same last name being repeated in the book and in the document. And now we also have a person named Zdravko Andabak.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but may I comment on this. I don't know if anybody reacted or not to this. But as I said, my assessment is that was a typo, a misspelling in the family name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have been told to correct this in the transcript, how Zdravko is spelled, as in Zdravko Andabak. It is Z-d-r-a-v-k-o. Zdravko is the first name; Andabak is the last name. Tell me, please, who is Mr. Jaganjac, and what is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely this document refers to Jasmin Jaganjac. Most likely the first name of this person is Jasmin. He was an officer of the army of Croatia who was active in this area, particularly in the city of Mostar and in this period, and originally he was a Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can move on to document number 16, please. Could you please be so kind as to look at the Croatian original. Please be so kind as to tell me, distinguished colleague, unless you have a more legible copy, this one is totally illegible.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say this is partly illegible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as we were able to read the English version, this also applies to the document which is obviously from another case. We can't see in it to whom it is addressed, who is writing to whom, and what president is meant.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think that you can see that. I think that you can see in the last page that it is addressed to President Tudjman, and it is signed and issued by President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in our letters, when the person is mentioned on the bottom, it means that that person is to be informed. It's not the right place for the addressee to be indicated. That's what we were taught in school. When you write a name on the bottom of the page, it means that that person is to receive a copy, to be informed. In this case, it means that Dr. Franjo Tudjman was to be informed of this letter. As for the English version, do you know what event it deals with? It's the events where the Muslims put up a barricade, and it's obvious it's from another case. Could you tell us -- Ahmici case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the last question. Once again, it wasn't a question. It went on for some five lines and then counsel went to a question. I object to statements by counsel which are not questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we believe that the cross-examination is on the right track. This is what we are going to hear for today, continuing with this witness. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik. Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think what Mr. Krsnik was taught in school is evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for this particular question, Mr. Krsnik, can you skip it? Or you may pose it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I won't even comment the latest objection by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dear colleague, I asked this question because we wanted to find out what this document is about. We do have the English version, but we were really unable to decipher this document that you provided us with, and that's why I'm trying to go into the contents. There seems to be a discrepancy, at least it's illegible, but to move on, regarding this document, did you study the Islamic Declaration by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the connection in between the Islamic Declaration and this document, but anyway, the answer is no, I didn't find it necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to know, whether you have studied it at all or not, because we are coming now to a different document, referring to mujahedins and so on and so forth. Of course, the question stands, what these documents have to do with the international armed conflict. Now we are coming to a number of documents that we will not trouble the Trial Chamber with. We will move on straight to document number 26. As you can see, all we have here is the English translation and a little bit in French. Is that the document that came from file IT-95 -- do you know that? My question was there was a case before this Tribunal, IT-95-12. Does this document come from this case too? Was it tendered? Was it admitted? Was it authenticated? Particularly because item 5, I believe, as you can see, item 5, refers to Gornji Vakuf, the Bosnian army, and its artillery. Who is this Major Luburic? What is this document about in the first place, and how is it relevant to international armed conflict? Except that, as we understood, the Bosnian army is opening artillery fire on Gornji Vakuf, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document refers to several different issues. I believe that the issue of interest for this testimony is the first paragraph, which says The LO team reported that many of Major Luburic's men had HV - which is army of Croatia - badges, and claimed to be Special Forces. So this is about, again, the presence of soldiers of the army of Croatia, this is in January of 1993, in the area of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me, in terms of consistency, have you ever come across the name of Major Luburic anywhere else, and who is this man?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have come across this name. Most likely, the first name of this person is Antun, and he was the commander of a special unit formally within the structure of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which citizenship he has? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever come across documents about his origins? Is he maybe a Canadian national?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me kindly, since you are an expert in international law, can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has never been tendered as an expert in international law. And again, it's beyond the scope of direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, by the way, that -- with due respect to the counsel, we also have some problem with this document, if we could ask some questions concerning this document. I understand this document claimed to be provided by the British government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And there is no -- any signature, no stamps, no other signs of the official characters. The source is completely unclear, so I would like to ask you to give us some explanations concerning this document 26.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do my best. That's right, there is no signature and no stamps of this kind. According to our records, in fact, the document was given to us by the British government. The British battalion of UNPROFOR was deployed in the relevant area, in the areas mentioned here, Kladanj, Novi Travnik, Vitez, et cetera. The units of the British battalion were producing regular reports. On the top, you can see Cheshire, which is the name of one such battalion. I mean, they were a replacement. The troops were moving. And at different periods, the same happened with the Spanish battalion. They had particular denominations. Cheshire was the name of one such British battalion. Then it says Milino. This is, I believe, again a misspelling. It should say "milinfosum," which was the regular elimination of the reports produced by the British forces, milinfosum. The reason why it doesn't contain signatures or stamps, I believe, is because it was an internal report, most likely from some officers in the ground to the headquarters of the British battalion. We will find the same in other documents as well. Being an internal report, we don't find such a science of identification of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How could we know that this document is reliable, about its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any certification provided by the providers or something like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What we have is, first, that it was given by us -- to us by the British authorities which, in our experience, they have been reliable. Besides that, what we have is a number of officers of the British battalion have been interviewed by us, and they have been questioned about their system of producing reports, their deployment, and their means to gain knowledge, how they were producing the reports. I can't tell you if the officer that produced this report in particular has been interviewed. This, I don't know. Honestly, I wanted to check that. But that has been the case with many documents provided by the British battalion as well as by the Spanish battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What we need is for some support to these documents, some other materials or testimonies or previous statement concerning the authenticity of this document, the sources of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. At this stage, this is as much as I can tell you. I would need to check again and verify we have interviewed the person who produced this document, which may be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik. I'm sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is precisely my intent, to get to know as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please open document number 28. As you can see on the first page of this document, paragraph number 2, it speaks about civil war. And this document, if I understand it correctly - and we have discussed it a little in the beginning as well - it refers to the Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and his actions based on the Geneva agreement. Do you know who was the Minister of Defence in 1992 and the beginning of 1993? I mean, the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your research and investigations, have you come across a decision by the Minister of Defence on the basis of the Geneva agreements, that on the territories where the Bosnian army, the Bosnian population is in the majority, the HVO should be -- should come under the command of the Bosnian army, and vice versa; on the territories where the HVO is in control, Bosnian units should subordinate themselves to the HVO command, based on the Geneva agreements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this as beyond the scope again. This is not a document that's in the collection. To ask this witness to speculate over every document he might have seen over the past -- since 1997, I think, is unfair to the witness and beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with the objections put forward by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely the reason behind my question, because on the second page of this document, in item 2, since we only have the English and the French versions, the last sentence is missing. And even we were able to understand the meaning of this. And that is why I wanted to have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Put your question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, does this document refer to provinces, as mentioned here, 3, 8, and 10? Does this document refer to that particular decision of the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will need a few seconds, if you allow me, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on the last page, item 4.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that I am not familiar with this -- such decision that you have mentioned. I am actually familiar with such a decision or such a proposal by the Croat side. Certainly the HVO side proposed that, which is, in certain provinces, the Bosnian army is subordinate to the HVO, and the other way around in other provinces. That is clear by many different sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, did I understand you correctly? Are you saying that the HVO opposed this decision of Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying is I don't know about such decision by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I just don't know. I do know that the HVO proposed such an arrangement in the terms that you have explained. That was an HVO proposal, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you touched upon Geneva documents from January and February, 1993, during your research?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to again object, Your Honours. It's beyond the scope, other documents not considered on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Krsnik, please concentrate on those documents tendered through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. However, these documents are inseparable, and for purposes of objective examination, and for the purpose of gaining complete knowledge, I think this should be clarified, but we will deal with that when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, doesn't this document too refer only to Central Bosnia, especially in view of the number of provinces? Doesn't this document refer to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that covers also Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me where Herzegovina is mentioned? Could you guide me through this document and show me which part is related to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In different parts. To begin with, Gornji Vakuf, in strict terms, to be accurate, is part of the northwest Herzegovina operational zone of the HVO. So for purposes of organisation of the HVO, Gornji Vakuf is considered, or was considered, by the HVO northwest Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've put it very correctly. It was considered. But is it geographically Herzegovina? I think not. I think geographically it is Central Bosnia. We keep forgetting that in this war, which made communication impossible, there was no communication between many enclaves. Did Herzegovina have communication with Central Bosnia at that time? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel just made two factual assertions in that last statement, for which there is no evidence in the record; no communications and there was no communication between many enclaves. There is no evidence in the record to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, this Chamber just said that you're on the right track, but now it seems to be de-tracked again. We have to go through this document, and we don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I'm doing my best. I'm doing all I can to have things clarified and show an objective picture. This witness visited Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in the relevant years, and my question was: Was there communication between Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Herzegovina and Central Bosnia at the time? Because it's a historical issue and it matters. I don't know whether it's clear to you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in short, the answer would be yes, but it was very difficult, it was very problematic, communication, due to the ongoing fight, combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I wanted the Trial Chamber to hear. Since we are talking about geographical units or zones of responsibility, it is understandable that there are certain deviations. And my last question regarding this document: You see that all this is based - and that is why I'm entitled to ask - it is all based on Geneva agreements. Do you agree that these documents originated after the Geneva agreements and that they are -- they explain what was happening on the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the key point in your question is agreement. The question is if there was such an agreement in Geneva. The documents follow from the Geneva negotiations. But to what extent the parties agreed, that -- well, that needs further explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, distinguished colleague. Are you aware whether the Vance-Owen Plan was signed? Consent was obtained from two parties, the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Muslims. It wasn't signed only by the Serbs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With due respect, you're putting to me this as a fact, and this is far from being established as a fact. If the question is if I agree with such allegation, the answer is no, I disagree with your allegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat. You disagree with the claim that Croats and Muslims signed the Vance-Owen Plan. Would I be right in coming to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, may I suggest to focus on the documents because this is explained in the documents contained in this collection. There is a report by the Secretary-General in which he explains what exactly happened, and the account of the Secretary-General is a more complex one. I think it would suffice with reading that document to understand what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your suggestions and assistance. Of course we will study these documents, but I was talking about a historical fact which took place. It was a very short question which called for a short answer. The documents are here and they speak for themselves. Otherwise, how could we understand the division into provinces and all that ensued later in 1995 and 1996? The conflict of 1995 and 1996 cannot be understood unless one has studied the Vance-Owen Plan and everything that happened in relation to that. Do you agree, at least, with that? When you researched these documents, did you come to the same conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that. Now let me comment briefly on this. The answer to such concern is in document number 27 of the collection. That is the report by the Secretary-General dated 18th of January. I think that that is enough to explain this point. And the answer was, the Croat side, Mr. Boban, signed right away, very willingly. The Bosnian side was hesitant and agreed with the constitutional principles but disagreed with the territorial arrangements. This you can read yourselves in document 27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, distinguished colleague. That's precisely what I was wondering about, what you mean by "ready," "willingly." The Vance-Owen Plan was a peace plan, it was a solution in the search for peace, and the Croatians were the first to sign it, and that is written in the general secretary -- Secretary-General's report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we seem to have reached a pattern in the last 15 or 20 minutes, which counsel is primarily making speeches. I simply refer you to the transcript of the last several questions. They are mostly speeches by counsel, followed, if followed at all, perhaps followed by -- excuse me, perhaps followed by a question, perhaps followed by no question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. We also believe that this question is not entirely relevant to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall abide by your guidelines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for document 29, please take a look at it, and I'm just going to ask you where the signature is on that document and whether it exists at all. Document number 29, [In English] Headquarters HVO. [Interpretation] There is French and English. As far as I can see, there is no Croatian version. Yes, we haven't got a version in Croatian. There is no signature. There is no stamp.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain you this. This seems to be the translation, translation that at the time was done by UNPROFOR themselves. Apparently, most likely, the headquarters of UNPROFOR translated such document and then sent it to the main quarters in Zagreb. This is a communication from Kiseljak to Zagreb. What I can tell you is that I'm familiar with this document and I have seen the original in Croat. I believe that it wouldn't be difficult really to produce the original of this document which is a well-known one. I would say actually signed by a brigadier, yes, Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me, I haven't had time at the moment to look in the exhibit list, but I think this is already an exhibit. It's already a Prosecution exhibit from January in the chronological set. And during that time period, I'm fairly sure we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have looked through all the documents and asked for them, but can I just ask you whether we could get this Croatian version -- the Croatian original. You said that you had it, so if you could please be so kind as to have it sent to us because, otherwise, how else can we have proof of all of this that you have been telling us? Because the easiest way to authenticate a source is to ask the person who signed it. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned several points. As for the request, this is a procedural matter, if this is possible from the procedural viewpoint. From the material viewpoint, it is not a problem because we are in possession of the Croat version with signature, stamps, and letterheads of the HVO. From the material viewpoint, it's not a problem. From the procedural viewpoint, it's not for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel and the Chamber may wish to look at Exhibit P216 which has the original Croat version attached with a seal signed by Milavoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these two documents require quite a bit of time. We have just heard about this, and then we will deal with this within our own research. And we'll see, Your Honours, whether this is an identical document. So we will continue doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we please move on to document 35 now. If we look at this document now, there is English and Croatian -- or actually, French and Croatian. However, again, there is no signature, let alone a stamp. The Croatian version, that is. If I'm not mistaken, the source is the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is no signature or stamp on it? It is a military order.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can explain you about this. This seems to be a cable version. This kind of communication was common within the structure of the HVO. I can tell you this because I have worked myself in the collections of the state archive of Croatia. It is a very common format for cable communications. And the information contained here seems to me a coherent, consistent. This commander -- this person, Zeljko Siljeg, was in fact, at this point in time, the commander of the operational zone with headquarters in Tomislavgrad. I can tell you that he was, himself, an officer of the army of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we please repeat the last name again for the transcript. Just the last name of this gentleman, this officer. You said Siljeg, Zeljko Siljeg, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said what is written in the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that he was an officer of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, Your Honours, by your leave I would like to spell the last name of this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] S-I-L-J-E-G.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when you sent telegrams, how are such telegrams sent in the A4 format, through the post? And what kind of force do they have in lower level units when it comes without a signature and without a stamp? Do you think the troops should go by that kind of thing, notably in times of war? What would happen if the enemy just put this in?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a regular means of communication in military structures. You would get this in this format, but you will have certain codes to identify, say, the frequency of transmission or the points of transmission of communications and so on. I can tell you that this is a very common means of communication, and the original documentary collections contain large numbers of these kind of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a document stating that Zeljko Siljeg is an officer of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Croatian army. Have you come across that kind of a document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually have several such documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Document Number 43. This is a document in English, right? And also a very short translation into French, if I'm not mistaken, very short. I think that, for the sake of fairness, it should have been translated into French as well, not to mention Croatian at this stage. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is a procedural comment, I have nothing to say about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because these are either documents of the army of the BH or the source is the army of the BH. Is the authenticity questionable?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said 43?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 43, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, there has been extensive testimony from the Spanish government about these documents. I don't understand the question of authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Yes, the SpaBat, the Spanish army. I confused some documents here. I do apologise to my colleague as well. I mean, what was SpaBat's source; the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I mean, for their document, was the source of their document the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did they write this document on the basis of what they received from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? However, my learned friend is right. We have discussed these matters extensively, so there's no point in discussing this any further with you. So by the leave of the Trial Chamber, I could move on to document 47.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 47. If you have leafed through this document, and if I understood correctly, June 1993, the 21st, it says that the B and H, if I understood it correctly, will use every opportunity to discredit the Serbs and Croats, capitalise on exposing the cooperation between the Serbs and Croats, and also the mujahedin and Guca Gora are referred to.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which page, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mujahedin are item 4, Central Bosnia; item 4(a), the second section under paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think that everybody can read this. First, the village of Guca Gora was ransacked, severe damage. And then in the next sentence, it says, The BH seem to regret this damage and were witnessed providing a clearance party of volunteers, et cetera, and interspersed [phoen] the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is -- just a minute, I'm sorry. We are all tired by now, aren't we? I just wanted to check the source, whether it is the Spanish army or the British army.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the level of credibility involved there, of these documents? Although I must say that my colleague, the Prosecutor, is right on that particular point. We have already dealt with this with witnesses from the Spanish battalion who testified here, so perhaps it is pointless for me to ask you about this as well with regard to these documents.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you briefly, in this collection, there are several documents of this kind, which is consolidated reports produced by the command of the headquarters of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak but then who were forwarded to the Spanish battalion, to the headquarters in Madrid in Spain. This means that these were created by UNPROFOR in Kiseljak, but they were given to us by the Spanish authorities in Madrid. If you want to go deeper about who collected originally the information, then we should review the area by the deployment of the battalions or eventually check UNMOs because it could have also been an UNMO team that provided the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Document 52, you've got your own notes as well, so there is no need for me to read this anyway. Is it consistent to assert, as it says here in this document, that it is possible that there are HV units, but, however, that that has not been checked out and that it is not certain? Have you found that in the course of your work in many documents precisely this kind of an assertion like what it says here in document 52? Would that be consistent? However, there is no French or Croatian translation.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you help me? In which part of the document is this stated?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 15th of July, 1993. I'm looking at my own notes. That's the date of the report.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see in this document what you were explaining.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm looking through it now. I'm looking through the document in order to think of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Point number 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes. It is point 8, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that fit in? Does this line of thinking fit in, of this particular source, that is? The European Monitoring Mission, ECMM. That's what it says here. Isn't there a vast majority of such documents, that is to say, unverified information on the presence of the HV?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this information is stated in a way that is not entirely assertive. It's not conclusive. It says only, "It is possible." Nevertheless, the reference to the HV and Split coincides with a number of other references contained in the collection. A number of documents refer to HV troops coming from Split. So this may help to corroborate, or this may lead us to believe that this might be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to interrupt. We also have some doubts concerning with this document. We believe that the source is completely unclear, and there is no signature. Would you make some explanation for us so that we have a better understanding of the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The explanation is similar to what I stated before, which is to say this seems to be an internal report of the monitoring mission. It seems that we received this in electronic format, and it is a print from such format, as far as I can see from this document. The Office of the Prosecutor has interviewed a number, actually many monitors, of the European Commission and has checked with monitors what was the proceedings, how were they gathering and producing the reports. I cannot state now if we have done such corroboration for this particular document. I will need to go back to the databases to verify that. I can certainly say that this has been done regularly with many documents, and a large number of monitors of the European Community have been interviewed by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand that, without corroborations for this document, it will be difficult for this Trial Chamber to admit it as evidence. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same pertains to document 54, where, under item D, the last sentence says the same thing. Item D, number 1, Mostar. That is page number 2 of document number 54. Like in the previous document, this information was not corroborated. There is no proof. So on what do you base your conclusion, that this could be consistent, that is?

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that this information is consistent with other documents included in the collection. The presence of troops of the HV has been mentioned in different documents from an early stage in 1992 and further on. So I think I can say that this is consistent with other documents of this same collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Distinguished colleague, perhaps my question was not quite clear. This document states that they cannot check this out, that they cannot verify this, that there is no proof of this, if I have understood the document correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, this gets us again into an area where we are arguing about the relevance or what the documents show. For instance, if at the end of the day, at the end of this trial, during the closing briefs or the closing argument, a large number of these documents are put together, along with the live testimony that the Chamber has heard, the Chamber may come to its ultimate conclusion that a particular sighting was not confirmed on a particular day on the totality of the evidence, including many documents that say, "We are pretty sure that the HV is in the area." This Chamber will frankly have a body of evidence available to it to make the ultimate conclusion that this particular writer didn't have on that day. The Chamber will be in a position to consider the totality of the evidence, including the vast witness testimony to date, which has sighted the presence of HV units, to make that determination. So it's unfair to argue about the weight to be given this particular document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as we come across many times in this cross-examination, we are only interested in the authenticity of the documents, the reliability of the sources and the credibility of the information contained in the document. Of course, you may not agree with the certain points in certain documents, but we are not debating on the substantive matters of this document, because this witness is just a documentary foundation witness. I thought we were on the right track, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I comment, please, on this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a point that I think may be relevant here. The fact is that they say, "Due to the lack of freedom that is still existing around the area of Mostar, this information cannot be checked and is therefore unconfirmed." To the best of my knowledge, the lack of freedom was due to the HVO restrictions, that they were denying access to the UNA officers to certain areas. So they were making a -- they were obstructing or making impossible the verification of the information getting into those areas. And the reason apparently for such restrictions were precisely that in those areas were units of the HV, besides certain crimes were committed in those areas. The best of my knowledge, that's what was happening in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've just heard a comment, and that's precisely what I wanted, because we can go straight to document 58, which speaks to the same thing, that they were unable to enter Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm now asking about the consistency which you insisted on in your examination-in-chief, and we have a number of documents here confirming that they did not have enough information to verify anything. If they were unable to enter Mostar, how can we make any claims or conclusions in this courtroom? That was my point. And thank you for your comment.

utterances.speaker: FRANCISCO AGUIRRE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can further explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
